subtype: Wow, ooh and ah in messages [Mismatch]
passage:
Tanvir: just sent you my sketch for the poster
Damini: wow.
Tanvir: ...is that good wow or bad wow 😬
Damini: what?? good wow!! why would I be sarcastic 😅
Tanvir: no full stop after it, and yesterday you said "wow" when I was late
Damini: yesterday I was annoyed about the bus, not you. this one is real. the colours are incredible ❤️
Tanvir: ok phew. text has no voice
Damini: true. next time I'll say more than one word
Tanvir: or call me
Damini: calling now

qa.q: What did Tanvir send to Damini?
qa.a: Tanvir sent a sketch for the poster.

qa.q: What was Tanvir worried about when Damini replied 'wow.'?
qa.a: Tanvir worried it was sarcasm, because the reply was one word with a full stop and Damini had said 'wow' at a bad moment yesterday. Damini's fuller message shows it was admiration.

qa.q: What could Damini do so a one-word text is not misread?
qa.a: Write a few more words or add a warm emoji, or call, so the feeling is clear.

qa.q: How might Damini have felt on learning Tanvir doubted the wow?
qa.a: Damini was probably surprised and a little worried about hurting Tanvir, and decided to call and add more words.

grounding: A young adult reads a text 'wow' as admiration, shock or sarcasm depending on tone, and clear words or a call prevent hurt.

subtype: Wow, ooh and ah in messages [Mismatch]
passage: In the small town of Pilibhit, Kishore sent Ujjwal a photo from the village fair of the new swing he'd repaired, and waited in the shade of the shop. The reply came quickly: "Wow." Just that. Kishore's face fell. Ujjwal had teased him about his carpentry before, and Kishore couldn't tell if this was pride or a jibe. He walked to the roof for signal and called. "Wow, as in genuinely, wow," Ujjwal said, laughing. "You got it to swing straight!" Kishore let out a breath. Ujjwal added that he'd typed it fast from the tractor and hadn't thought how flat it would look. They agreed that next time he'd type more words.

qa.q: What did Kishore send Ujjwal a photo of?
qa.a: Kishore sent a photo of the new swing he had repaired.

qa.q: What was Kishore feeling when he read the one-word reply?
qa.a: Kishore was unsure and a bit hurt, because he could not tell whether 'Wow' was pride or a jibe after earlier teasing. The call showed it was admiration.

qa.q: What could Kishore do next time a short reply feels unclear?
qa.a: Ask what the reply meant or call, as he did, and tell Ujjwal that short texts can sound flat.

qa.q: How might Ujjwal have felt hearing that Kishore doubted him?
qa.a: Ujjwal was probably surprised and sorry, since he had typed fast from the tractor and meant real admiration.

grounding: A young adult reads 'wow' in a message as admiration or sarcasm, and a follow-up call clears it.

subtype: Louder, higher voice in excitement or anger [Interpreting]
passage:
Dear Lalremsiami,

Do you remember Sunday's dinner at my place? I've been thinking about how loud everyone got. When Ritu told us she had passed her viva, her voice shot up, everyone talked over each other, and I was laughing so hard my eyes watered. It was the loud of joy. Ten minutes later, my brother's voice went just as loud and high about the water bill and I felt my shoulders go up. Same volume, very different feeling. The words and his face told me it was anger, so I lowered my own voice and said we could talk later. He stepped out for a minute.

I hope you're well. Write soon.

Damini

qa.q: What good news did Ritu share at dinner?
qa.a: Ritu said she had passed her viva.

qa.q: What was Damini feeling when the brother's voice went loud and high?
qa.a: Damini felt tense, with her shoulders going up, because the words and his face pointed to anger. The volume alone could not tell Damini, since the joy earlier was equally loud.

qa.q: What could Damini do if a raised angry voice feels unsafe?
qa.a: Stay calm, speak more quietly, suggest talking later, and step back or leave if it feels unsafe.

qa.q: How might Damini's brother have felt when Damini suggested talking later?
qa.a: He may have felt frustrated but also given a chance to cool down, since he stepped out for a minute.

grounding: A young adult hears louder, higher voices in both excitement and anger and uses words, face and context to tell them apart.

subtype: Louder, higher voice in excitement or anger [Interpreting]
passage: You asked what it's like living with three friends, Farida, so here's one thing I've noticed. Deepika here. When we all get excited, we get louder and our voices go up. Last week when Pooja got her internship offer, the flat sounded like a fair. Loud, high, everyone laughing. Then on Friday, Meera and Ishita argued about who used the last of the milk, and they were exactly as loud and high, but their faces were stiff and the words were sharp. I felt my stomach knot. I didn't try to fix it. I said quietly that I'd make tea for everyone, and I left the room for a bit. Later they laughed about it. I still check the words and the face, never just the volume.

qa.q: What did Pooja get last week?
qa.a: Pooja got an internship offer.

qa.q: What did Deepika feel during the milk argument?
qa.a: Deepika felt uneasy, with a knotted stomach, since the loud, high voices came with stiff faces and sharp words. Deepika read anger from more than volume, but could not be certain what each person felt.

qa.q: What could Deepika do when housemates argue loudly?
qa.a: Stay calm, avoid taking sides, offer tea in a quiet voice and step out if it gets too tense.

qa.q: How might Meera and Ishita have felt about being interrupted with tea?
qa.a: They may have felt a little embarrassed but also cooled down, since they laughed about it later.

grounding: A young adult hears friends louder and higher when excited and when angry, and words, face and context decide.

subtype: Varying pitch for persuasion and presentation [Regulating]
passage: The debating hall at the Kolkata college was warm and half asleep. When Alka stood up for the final round, Bhupen, in the third row, saw people shift in their seats. She began in a low, steady voice, slowed on the key figures, let the pause hang, then raised her pitch when she reached the surprising bit. The room leaned in. Bhupen noticed that when she described the village clinic, her voice softened, and when she turned to the opponents' numbers it sharpened. It didn't feel staged. He couldn't say what she was feeling underneath, only that it held him. Afterwards he asked her whether she planned the pauses. Alka smiled and said not exactly.

qa.q: In which row was Bhupen sitting?
qa.a: Bhupen was in the third row.

qa.q: What might Alka be aiming for with her changing pitch, and how sure can Bhupen be?
qa.a: Alka varied pitch and pace, slowing on key figures, pausing, and softening for the village clinic, which kept the room engaged. Bhupen could only guess at her inner state and said so.

qa.q: What could a speaker do to avoid sounding flat in a debate?
qa.a: Vary pace and pitch naturally to fit the content, pausing before key points, rather than adding theatrical effects.

qa.q: How might the opponents have seen Alka's delivery?
qa.a: They might have found it persuasive and a little unsettling, since the changes matched the content and felt sincere rather than staged.

grounding: A young adult varies pitch and pace in a debate to keep listeners engaged, and the variety feels natural rather than theatrical.

subtype: Varying pitch for persuasion and presentation [Regulating]
passage:
Monday. Divyansh practised his interview answers in the hostel corridor. Mohit, a friend, listened and said, "You sound like you're reading a bill." Divyansh's voice was flat and fast, one long line.

Thursday. Divyansh tried again, this time recording himself. He slowed down, paused before the main point and let his voice rise when he talked about his project. Mohit said it sounded better, but at one point Divyansh tried a dramatic whisper and it felt fake. They both laughed and he dropped it.

Following Tuesday. In the real interview, Divyansh kept his natural variety and the panel nodded. Mohit heard the good news that evening.

qa.q: Where did Divyansh practise his interview answers on Monday?
qa.a: Divyansh practised in the hostel corridor.

qa.q: What did Divyansh feel about the dramatic whisper?
qa.a: Divyansh likely felt a bit silly, since the whisper sounded fake, and laughing about it with Mohit made it easy to drop.

qa.q: What steps helped Divyansh improve?
qa.a: He recorded himself, slowed down, paused before the main point and let his voice rise naturally when he spoke about the project.

qa.q: How did Mohit see Divyansh's first attempt?
qa.a: Mohit said it sounded like reading a bill, since the voice was flat and fast in one long line.

grounding: A young adult varies pitch and pace to avoid sounding flat in an interview, keeping natural variety rather than theatrics.

subtype: Resonant and confident speaking voice [Expressing]
passage: I'm Kavitha, and the first time I felt my own voice work for me was at a scholarship interview. My hands were cold, my heart was thudding, and Ayesha, my friend, had told me before I went in, "Feel your feet, breathe from your belly, speak like you're telling a friend." So I sat tall, breathed out slowly and started. My voice came out lower and steadier than I expected. The panel leaned in. I still felt nervous inside. It was steady on the outside, though, which surprised me. Later Ayesha said I sounded composed, and I said I wasn't at all. So a steady voice doesn't always mean a calm mind, I think, but it helped me.

qa.q: What did Ayesha tell Kavitha before the interview?
qa.a: Ayesha told Kavitha to feel the feet on the floor, breathe from the belly and speak as if telling a friend.

qa.q: What was Kavitha feeling under that steady voice?
qa.a: Kavitha was nervous, with cold hands and a thudding heart, even though Kavitha's voice sounded composed. The steady sound came from breath and posture, not from a calm mind.

qa.q: What could Kavitha do before the next interview?
qa.a: Sit tall, breathe out slowly and feel the feet on the floor, as Kavitha did, and practise speaking as if telling a friend.

qa.q: How did Ayesha see Kavitha's voice?
qa.a: Ayesha heard it as composed and did not know how nervous Kavitha felt inside.

grounding: A young adult speaks with a resonant steady voice in an interview, which can signal composure even when nervous, and breath and posture help.

subtype: Resonant and confident speaking voice [Expressing]
passage: Note from Ms. Gopika, faculty mentor. On Friday I sat on the panel for the final-year project presentations. Arnab walked to the front, stood with his feet apart and took a long breath before starting. His voice was deep, even and clear across the hall, and he made eye contact with each examiner in turn. The room settled. I noticed his hand around the clicker was white at the knuckles, and afterwards he told me he'd been dreading it all week. So the steady voice was partly practice and partly effort. I told him what I saw and suggested he keep the breathing, and Arnab said he would do exactly that in the next viva.

qa.q: Where did Arnab stand while starting?
qa.a: Arnab stood at the front with his feet apart.

qa.q: What did the white knuckles suggest about Arnab's feelings?
qa.a: They suggested Arnab was nervous under the steady voice, which he confirmed by saying he had dreaded the presentation. The voice showed composure, but not the whole picture.

qa.q: What could Arnab keep doing in the next viva?
qa.a: Keep the long breath and steady stance before speaking, since they helped his voice come out even and clear.

qa.q: How might the examiners have seen Arnab's voice?
qa.a: They probably took it as composed and confident, as the room settled, without seeing the tight grip on the clicker.

grounding: A young adult presents with a resonant steady voice that signals composure, though nervous people can sound steady too.

subtype: Trembling voice in high-stakes talk [Interpreting]
passage: Irfan, let me tell you about something from my second year as a lecturer. Abhinav here. A student called Sheetal stood up to give her first seminar and her voice shook so badly the whole room went quiet. I thought, she's terrified. Some people looked away. I didn't say anything for a moment, and I smiled. Then she said, "Sorry, this is about my grandfather's fields, and I've never spoken about them." It was grief and pride, not fear. I asked whether she wanted a minute, and she took a sip of water and went on, steadier. I never assume from a shaking voice now. I wait, I stay warm, and I ask.

qa.q: What was Sheetal's seminar about?
qa.a: Sheetal's seminar was about her grandfather's fields.

qa.q: What did Abhinav first think was behind the trembling voice?
qa.a: Abhinav first thought Sheetal was terrified, but her words showed it was grief and pride. So the shaking voice could carry several feelings.

qa.q: What could a teacher do when a student's voice trembles?
qa.a: Wait, stay warm, and ask if the student wants a minute, instead of assuming weakness.

qa.q: How might Sheetal have felt when some people looked away?
qa.a: Sheetal may have felt exposed and even more nervous, since she was speaking about something personal.

grounding: An elder recalls a trembling voice that looked like fear but was grief and pride, and the wise response is to wait, be warm and ask.

subtype: Trembling voice in high-stakes talk [Interpreting]
passage: The projector died five minutes before Disha's group presentation at the Nairobi conference, and rain hammered on the tin roof. Disha stepped up without slides, and her voice trembled from the first sentence. Mehak, seated at the back, worried it meant panic. Others whispered. But when Disha began talking about her grandmother's market stall, which was why she'd chosen the topic, her voice cracked and steadied again. Mehak realised the shake might be a mix of the missing slides and something deeply personal. At the break, Mehak brought her a cup of tea and asked, "How are you feeling?" Disha said, "Shaky, but I'm glad I told it." Mehak nodded and stayed beside her.

qa.q: What died five minutes before Disha's group presentation?
qa.a: The projector died.

qa.q: What did Mehak first think about Disha's trembling voice?
qa.a: Mehak worried it meant panic, and then saw it might also come from something deeply personal. Mehak had to ask, since the tremble alone could not say.

qa.q: What did Mehak do that helped?
qa.a: Mehak brought tea at the break and asked 'How are you feeling?', instead of assuming weakness.

qa.q: What was it like for Disha to speak without slides?
qa.a: Disha felt shaky, but glad to tell the story, so the missing slides and the personal topic together made her voice tremble.

grounding: A listener hears a trembling voice under a complication of a dead projector and asks rather than assuming.

subtype: Measured pace in interviews and presentations [Regulating]
passage: You asked how I stayed so calm in that panel interview, Vaibhav, and honestly it was on purpose. Yamini here. I'd noticed that when I'm nervous I speed up until I'm tripping over words. So before going in I decided to slow down. When they asked about my project, I paused for a breath, said "Let me structure this" and gave it in three parts, with a short pause between each. One of the panel members wrote something down. But I nearly overdid it. When they asked about my hobbies I was so slow that the woman on the left glanced at her watch. So I picked up the pace a bit. Slow for the hard bits, natural for the light ones.

qa.q: How many parts did Yamini give the project answer in?
qa.a: Yamini gave the answer in three parts.

qa.q: Why did Yamini decide to slow down before the interview?
qa.a: Yamini knew that nerves bring speeding up and tripping over words, so the aim was to sound organised. Overdoing it drew a glance at the watch, so Yamini adjusted.

qa.q: What could Yamini do to fit the pace to the room?
qa.a: Keep pauses for the harder answers and speak at a more natural speed for lighter topics.

qa.q: How might the panel member have felt during Yamini's very slow answer?
qa.a: The panel member may have felt time pressure or lost interest, as the glance at the watch suggests, though it may also have been ordinary schedule-checking.

grounding: A young adult keeps a measured pace with deliberate pauses in an interview and adjusts when slowing too much.

subtype: Measured pace in interviews and presentations [Regulating]
passage: Ganga's turn in the seminar came just after tea. I'm Tushar, and I was seated next to her. She started very slowly, pausing after each point, and by the second minute a couple of students were fidgeting. Someone yawned. I honestly thought she was unprepared, and I nearly leaned over to whisper. But her slides were tidy and her answers to the first question were clear and organised. Then the professor asked about the second graph and she picked up speed, talking more easily. I don't know if it was nerves, or a plan, or just how she thinks. The professor nodded, and afterwards Ganga told me she'd practised the slow start to sound calm.

qa.q: Who was seated next to Ganga in the seminar?
qa.a: Tushar was seated next to Ganga.

qa.q: What did Tushar first think when Ganga started so slowly?
qa.a: Tushar thought she might be unprepared, but her tidy slides and clear answers showed otherwise. Tushar admits it is hard to tell if it was nerves, a plan or her thinking style.

qa.q: What could Ganga do to keep listeners engaged with a slow pace?
qa.a: Match the pace to the room, picking up speed on easier points and saving the long pauses for the key ideas.

qa.q: How might the fidgeting students have felt?
qa.a: They may have felt bored or impatient at the slow start, though it was a cue, not proof of disinterest in the topic.

grounding: An observer sees a measured pace with pauses look organised, but slowing too much can look like disinterest.

subtype: Rhythm across languages and dialects [Mismatch]
passage: In a Manchester cafe, Jamal listened to his new classmate Bilal, who had grown up in Lagos and Karachi, speak at an astonishing speed, the words rolling up and down like music. Jamal felt lost and a bit annoyed. He'd assumed Bilal was rushing to impress him or was not listening. But when Bilal paused and asked about Jamal's own hometown, his questions were sharp and kind. Jamal realised the rhythm was simply how Bilal talked, in a tune shaped by two homes. Jamal asked Bilal to slow down a touch and Bilal laughed and did. Jamal also decided never to guess someone's attitude from their speech rhythm alone.

qa.q: Where did Bilal grow up?
qa.a: Bilal grew up in Lagos and Karachi.

qa.q: What did Jamal feel while listening to Bilal at first?
qa.a: Jamal felt lost and a bit annoyed, assuming Bilal was rushing or not listening. Bilal's sharp, kind questions showed the assumption was wrong.

qa.q: What could Jamal do when someone's speech rhythm is hard to follow?
qa.a: Ask politely for a slower pace and listen to the content, not just the rhythm.

qa.q: How might Bilal have felt when asked to slow down?
qa.a: Bilal laughed and slowed down, which suggests he took it kindly, though he may have felt a touch self-conscious about his accent.

grounding: A young adult finds that speech rhythm differs across accents and judging attitude from rhythm alone is unfair.

subtype: Rhythm across languages and dialects [Mismatch]
passage: In the Pune call centre training room, the trainer had asked Minakshi and Bhavna to role-play a customer call. Minakshi's English carried the sing-song rhythm of her Malayalam mother tongue, quick and rising. Bhavna, who spoke Marathi at home, started to think Minakshi sounded over-friendly and a bit unserious. She gave a small frown. Then the trainer played back the recording and pointed out that Minakshi's answers had been accurate, patient and complete. Bhavna felt her face go warm. In the tea break she said sorry for the frown. Minakshi smiled and said, "It happens all the time. That's just how my speech moves."

qa.q: Which language does Minakshi speak at home?
qa.a: Minakshi's mother tongue is Malayalam.

qa.q: What did Bhavna feel when she heard the sing-song rhythm?
qa.a: Bhavna felt unsure and thought Minakshi sounded over-friendly and unserious, then realised the answers were accurate, and felt embarrassed. The judgement came from rhythm alone.

qa.q: What could a trainer do about speech rhythm in a call centre?
qa.a: Judge the accuracy and care of the answers, and remind trainees that rhythm and accent differ without showing intelligence or attitude.

qa.q: How might Minakshi have felt about Bhavna's frown?
qa.a: Minakshi probably felt used to it, since she said it happens all the time, though it may still sting a bit.

grounding: A young adult learns a sing-song rhythm can be normal for the speaker, and that judging intelligence or attitude from rhythm is unfair.

subtype: Strategic pause and long silence [Regulating]
passage: The negotiation for the flat was down to the last ten minutes before the train, and the owner wanted a higher rent. Rain drummed on the window. Amandeep looked at the number on the paper, said nothing for a slow breath, and let the silence sit. Jatin, her friend beside her, felt his palms sweat and wanted to fill the gap. Instead he held his tongue. The owner shifted, then said, "Maybe we could go a little lower." Amandeep smiled and nodded, and later told Jatin she'd used the pause to think, not to pressure. In some rooms she'd have spoken sooner, she said, but this owner seemed to value a thoughtful reply.

qa.q: What was drumming on the window?
qa.a: Rain was drumming on the window.

qa.q: What was Jatin feeling during the silence?
qa.a: Jatin felt uneasy, with sweating palms, and wanted to fill the gap. He held back, which shows he trusted Amandeep's pause.

qa.q: What could Amandeep do if a long silence feels too heavy for the other person?
qa.a: Give a short sentence to acknowledge the point, such as saying she is thinking about it, to keep the room comfortable.

qa.q: How might the owner have seen the silence?
qa.a: The owner may have felt some pressure, then shifted and offered a lower rent, or may have taken it as a thoughtful pause; the setting and the person shape the reading.

grounding: A young adult uses a brief pause in a negotiation to think and let a point land, with a time-pressure complication.

subtype: Strategic pause and long silence [Regulating]
passage: At the marketing agency in Mumbai, Vijay was interviewing Sarita for a junior role. He asked her about a failed campaign. Sarita didn't answer at once. She looked at the table for three or four seconds, then said, "I think the mistake was mine. I didn't test the timing." Vijay found the pause made the answer more honest. Sarita felt her heart beat in the quiet and hoped it didn't look like she'd forgotten. After the interview she said her aunt had taught her that a moment of silence shows respect for a question. Vijay realised he'd felt slightly uncomfortable in the gap, but decided that it was his own habit and not a sign of weakness.

qa.q: What did Vijay ask Sarita about?
qa.a: Vijay asked Sarita about a failed campaign.

qa.q: What was Sarita feeling during the pause?
qa.a: Sarita felt nervous, her heart beating in the quiet, and hoped she didn't look like she had forgotten. The pause was meant to show thought and respect for the question.

qa.q: What could an interviewer do when a candidate pauses?
qa.a: Wait comfortably rather than jumping in, since the pause may be thinking or respect.

qa.q: How did Vijay see the pause in the end?
qa.a: Vijay found it made the answer more honest, and saw his discomfort as his own habit, not Sarita's weakness.

grounding: A young adult in an interview uses a brief pause to think, and the setting shapes how a silence is read.

subtype: Chanting, devotional singing and protest songs [Mismatch]
passage: At the village temple fair in Rajasthan, Madhav joined the evening bhajan. The drums beat fast and the whole crowd sang the chorus, and he felt the joy of his grandmother's faith. Later that week, on the road to the district office, Shankar led the farmers' march with a chant in a similar drumbeat, and Madhav caught himself clapping along. But something in Shankar's tone was different. It was stern, hard and angry about the delayed compensation. Madhav's chest tightened. The rhythm was almost the same, but the meaning was not. He listened to the words before joining, and stayed near the edge until he was sure what the group was asking.

qa.q: Where did Madhav join the evening bhajan?
qa.a: Madhav joined it at the village temple fair in Rajasthan.

qa.q: What did Madhav feel when he heard the march chant?
qa.a: Madhav felt his chest tighten, sensing anger behind a rhythm that sounded like the bhajan. He listened to the words first, because the beat alone did not tell him.

qa.q: What could a young person do before joining a chant in a crowd?
qa.a: Listen to the words, see what the group is asking for, and join only if they agree and it is safe.

qa.q: How might Shankar have seen the chanting?
qa.a: Shankar sounded stern and angry about the delayed compensation, so the chant was a way of asking to be heard rather than of showing faith or joy.

grounding: A young adult meets the same drumbeat in devotional singing and a protest chant, showing that context decides its meaning.

subtype: Chanting, devotional singing and protest songs [Mismatch]
passage: At the Seoul football stadium, Soo-ah stood beside her friend Leila and sang the team song with thousands of others, arms locked, her voice ringing off the roof. It was pure fun. Leila, who was visiting from Tunis, joined in the parts she knew. A week later, on a cold evening, they stood at a candlelight gathering where people sang a slow song for the workers who had died in a factory fire. The tune was almost the same as the stadium one, but slower. Soo-ah's voice was quiet and rough. Leila stood still and listened, and put a hand on Soo-ah's shoulder when it seemed welcome. Soo-ah nodded.

qa.q: Where did Soo-ah sing the team song?
qa.a: Soo-ah sang the team song at the Seoul football stadium.

qa.q: What was Soo-ah feeling at the candlelight gathering?
qa.a: Soo-ah was probably sad and heavy-hearted, since her voice was quiet and rough while singing for the workers who died. It could also have been anger, since protest and grief can share a tune.

qa.q: How could Leila show respect at the gathering?
qa.a: Listen quietly, follow the group's mood, and offer a touch only if it seems welcome.

qa.q: How might the families of the workers see the singing?
qa.a: They might find it comforting that others remember their loss, though grief is personal and each person may feel it differently.

grounding: A young adult sings in a stadium and in a mourning gathering with a similar tune, and context and respect for the group matter.

subtype: Formal introductions and self-introduction [Expressing]
passage: You asked how I got through that first orientation morning, Sarika. Lavanya here. I was the only one who didn't know anyone, and the coordinator said, "Introduce yourself, one line each." I felt my knees go soft. But I'd practised with my sister the night before: name, course, one interest. So I stood up, looked at the group and said, "Hello, I'm Lavanya, I'm joining the design course, and I like drawing old buses." Someone laughed, warm, and a boy said he loved buses too. After that I wasn't a stranger. Later my roommate from Denmark said they just use first names for teachers, while I'd called mine "Professor Rao" and she'd stared. So I learned to watch how people address each other.

qa.q: What does Lavanya like to draw?
qa.a: Lavanya likes drawing old buses.

qa.q: What was Lavanya feeling when standing up for the introduction?
qa.a: Lavanya was nervous, as the soft knees show, but practising a short line beforehand helped. The warm laugh from others suggests Lavanya was received kindly.

qa.q: What could a new student do before an introduction round?
qa.a: Prepare a short line with name, course and one interest, and watch how people in the room use titles.

qa.q: How might the roommate from Denmark have seen 'Professor Rao'?
qa.a: The roommate stared because in her country teachers go by first name, so the title may have looked overly formal.

grounding: A young adult introduces themselves with name, role and a short line about interests, and norms for titles differ across cultures.

subtype: Formal introductions and self-introduction [Expressing]
passage: Note to my study circle, from Gargi. At the campus club fair I sat by the table and watched Neelam approach the robotics stall. She said, in a clear voice, "Hi, I'm Neelam, I'm in second-year electronics, and I'm interested in drones." She put out her hand for a handshake and looked at the club president. He smiled and said he'd never met a second-year who knew what a servo was. It seemed to work. But another stall organiser, older, kept looking at her folder and didn't meet her eyes for long, and I couldn't tell if it was shyness, culture or boredom. Neelam didn't seem to mind. She went on to the next stall with the same clear line.

qa.q: What year is Neelam in?
qa.a: Neelam is in the second year of electronics.

qa.q: What did Gargi think about the older organiser looking at the folder?
qa.a: Gargi couldn't tell whether it was shyness, culture or boredom, since eye contact norms differ. Neelam didn't seem to mind, so it may not have been a snub.

qa.q: What could Neelam keep doing at future stalls?
qa.a: Keep her introduction clear and short with name, year and interest, and read how each person likes to greet.

qa.q: How might the club president have felt?
qa.a: The club president seemed pleased and impressed, as his smile and comment show.

grounding: A young adult introduces self with name, role and interest, and eye contact and title norms differ across cultures.
